extracted.intended_audience: cognitive scientists, computational humor researchers, and AI/cognitive-architecture researchers interested in modeling or understanding humor
extracted.subtask_description: A theory-driven framework describing cognitive and emotional processes that produce humor (mirth) and guidance for computational implementations (e.g., pun recognition). Emphasizes a dual-process, appraisal-based sequence and empirical phenomena that any model should account for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (expectation violation triggers System 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first stage of humor comprehension: an expectation created by associative System 1 is violated, leading to surprise which engages deliberate System 2 processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is a fast appraisal (novelty/expectation violation) processed in regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Examples: in puns the punchline violates the automatic meaning (e.g., 'gifted child' + 'paid for you'). Surprise is slightly negative and is the signal that triggers reflective processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection (System 2 makes sense of the surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second stage: System 2 is engaged by surprise and performs deliberate, effortful processing to reconcile or reinterpret the stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection uses working memory and is slow and tiring (correlates: dilated pupils, increased heart rate). It attempts to find alternative meanings or attributions (e.g., double meanings in puns) so that the surprising stimulus becomes intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal (appraise the stimulus as irrelevant/not worth further processing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third stage: after reflection, the surprising stimulus is appraised as trivial, fake, or not worthy of further attention, leading to deactivation of System 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismissal is distinct from mere resolution: a riddle whose answer yields genuine learning is resolved but not dismissed and therefore not funny. Models should include a fast relevance appraisal (EMA/CPM) that can mark an event as non-threatening/irrelevant to enable dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation / Trampoline effect (relief leads to mirth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth stage: deactivation of System 2 and re-adjustment from a slightly negative (surprised/strained) state to neutral or positive produces amplified positive emotion (mirth) — the 'trampoline' effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accumulated negative affect from surprise and cognitive effort is relieved rapidly upon dismissal, producing an overcompensating positive burst. This effect can be compounded by other appraisals (e.g., superiority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor requires dismissal, not merely incongruity-resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when the surprise is not only resolved but appraised as irrelevant/not worth further processing; mere resolution (as in puzzles) that produces learning does not produce mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction explains why riddles/puzzles are often not funny despite having incongruity and resolution: if the resolution is an opportunity for learning rather than trivialization, laughter does not follow. The theory refines incongruity-resolution by adding the dismissal requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority (compounding factor, not necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling superior (social inappropriateness, mockery) can amplify humor but is not a defining feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superiority can compound mirth by adding social pleasure downstream of the four-stage process; however jokes without identifiable inferiority (e.g., some puns) can still be funny. Superiority typically operates later and enhances compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation refinement: 'benign' must be perceived as fake/irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation must be appraised as benign in the sense that it is recognized as fake/irrelevant (i.e., not an opportunity for learning or threat) for mirth to arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many daily benign violations (bus late, computer unresponsive) are not funny because they do not get appraised as 'fake' or trivial in the dismissal sense. The appraisal for benignness is typically slower (social norm checks) and compounds but does not itself create surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency and processing speed increase funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Faster realization/interpretation of the joke's meaning (processing fluency) leads to higher funniness ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topolinski (2014) shows faster meaning realization correlates with funniness; in the proposed mechanism, rapid reflection and quick dismissal shorten the negative interval and increase the trampoline effect. Computational models should prioritize quick re-interpretation following the surprise signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition effects: moderate repetition can increase, high repetition decreases funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition can initially increase perceived joy (due to fluency) but prolonged exposure trains System 1 and eventually 'wears out' the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies (Belch & Belch, Zhang & Zinkhan, Picard) show low-to-medium repetition may boost ratings, second viewings can increase joy, but continued exposure reduces novelty as System 1 adapts. Models should capture both fluency gains and long-term learning in System 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke crafting balance: difficulty must straddle System 1 and System 2
rubrics_metrics.description: A good joke must be difficult enough that System 1 does not immediately understand it, yet easy enough that System 2 can resolve it quickly without prolonged strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because System 2 is slow and effortful, the teller must 'walk a thin line' — a joke that is too easy yields no surprise, too hard yields prolonged strain and reduced mirth. This asymmetry explains why joke-telling skill can signal intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social context and shared appraisals amplify humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor appreciation is strongly influenced by social setting; presence of others or shared appraisals increases funniness and may serve social-bonding functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show jokes are funnier with others present; laughter signals shared values and can indicate social alignment. Models or evaluations of humor should account for social amplification effects and normative/appraisal alignment between participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences (working memory, cognitive style) affect appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Variability in working memory capacity and reflective tendencies influences how quickly System 2 can resolve surprises and therefore affects humor preference (e.g., high vs low comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals with lower working memory may take longer to resolve complex jokes and thus find them less funny due to reduced processing fluency. The dual-process account predicts systematic individual differences in humor appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frustration smiles and reappraisal-driven humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor-like positive affect (frustration smiles) can be produced via reappraisal/coping strategies that trivialize a negative stimulus, following the same surprise-reflection-dismissal-compensation pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In impossibility/frustration tasks, participants may reappraise failures as bugs/pranks, dismissing threat and producing mirth. Any mechanism that effectuates dismissal (including emotion-regulation reappraisal) can produce humor-like responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational modeling requirements: integrate expectation violation, appraisals, and dual-process timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational systems that recognize or generate humor should model expectation-violation detection, fast appraisals (novelty/relevance), slower reflective inference (System 2), dismissal/reappraisal, and the timing needed for compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper suggests compatibility with major cognitive architectures and that architectures built around expectation violation are a good starting point. For pun recognition, models must represent multiple meanings, detect surprise, rapidly reframe meaning, evaluate relevance, and produce an affective output contingent on dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neuroscientific temporal sequence as empirical validation target
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical validation should show a temporal sequence consistent with the theory: early surprise/ACC activation, followed by detection/resolution activations (posterior temporal / inferior frontal), and later appreciation-related activation (e.g., insula) associated with compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moran et al. (2004) found two phases in fMRI studies (detection/resolution then appreciation). Wessel et al. link surprise/expectation violation to ACC. Models/theories should be compatible with these observed neural timings and activations.
